The intent of the security fix is to disable SQL expressions by default while allowing operators to re-enable them via the existing feature flag (as documented in the linked PR #81666). As written, the flag is dead code and the check `if !enabled { return ... }` at the call site (line 129-132) is misleading. The function should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (i.e., return true only when the flag is enabled), so that the gate actually respects the toggle. Without this fix, operators who legitimately need SQL expressions (and have the flag enabled) cannot use them, and the code misrepresents the security posture."

The PR description says the goal is to move the security fix into the repo while keeping the feature flag functional, but this stub makes the feature completely non-functional rather than gated. The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and the intended \"no data\" semantics (which typically signal to the frontend/alerting that the query returned no data points, distinct from an empty table) are lost. This is a pre-existing bug in the file (not introduced by this diff), but it is in the direct path of the SQL expression feature being modified by this PR, and it means the `if frame.Rows() == 0` block should either be removed or the unconditional assignment should be made conditional (`else`)."

Telling users it is \"not implemented\" will cause confusion and incorrect troubleshooting (users may believe the query type is unsupported rather than disabled by configuration). The message should say something like \"SQL expressions are disabled\" or \"sqlExpressions feature is disabled\" so that operators understand they need to enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle (and accept the security implications) to use it."

findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false, making the feature-flag check dead code and the flag non-functional
findings.body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then immediately returns `false` in both branches (`if enabled { return false }` followed by `return false`). This means the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle has no effect: SQL expressions are always rejected with "sqlExpressions is not implemented" regardless of whether the flag is enabled. The intent of the security fix is to disable SQL expressions by default while allowing operators to re-enable them via the existing feature flag (as documented in the linked PR #81666). As written, the flag is dead code and the check `if !enabled { return ... }` at the call site (line 129-132) is misleading. The function should return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (i.e., return true only when the flag is enabled), so that the gate actually respects the toggle. Without this fix, operators who legitimately need SQL expressions (and have the flag enabled) cannot use them, and the code misrepresents the security posture.

findings.title: Stub DB methods return 'not implemented' errors, so SQL expressions fail at runtime even if the reader gate is bypassed

The PR description says the goal is to move the security fix into the repo while keeping the feature flag functional, but this stub makes the feature completely non-functional rather than gated. Either the DuckDB dependency should be retained behind the flag, or the stub should be clearly documented as permanently disabling the feature (in which case the flag check in reader.go should be removed entirely rather than kept as dead code).

The `NoData` branch is therefore dead code and the intended "no data" semantics (which typically signal to the frontend/alerting that the query returned no data points, distinct from an empty table) are lost. findings.title: SQL string escaping by doubling single quotes is insufficient and leaves an injection path if TablesList is ever reachable
findings.body: `TablesList` builds a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` after only replacing single quotes with doubled single quotes (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`). This escaping does not account for backslash escapes (DuckDB/SQL string literals interpret `\'` as an escaped quote, so a payload ending in a backslash can break out of the string literal), and it is applied to user-controlled SQL before it is passed to `RunCommands`. In the current state this code path is unreachable in production because `NewSQLCommand` is gated off in `pkg/expr/reader.go` and the stub `DB.RunCommands` returns "not implemented", but the function remains exported and callable, and the escaping is a classic SQL-injection anti-pattern. If the feature flag gate is fixed (see related finding) or if this function is called from any other path, an attacker-controlled `rawSQL` value could inject arbitrary DuckDB commands (which, per CVE-2024-9264, can lead to RCE/LFI via DuckDB extensions and file access). The correct fix is to not build SQL by string concatenation at all — use a parameterized query or pass the SQL text via a bound parameter — and to ensure this code is unreachable unless the feature is explicitly enabled.

findings.title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading — the feature exists but is disabled
findings.body: When SQL expressions are rejected, the error returned to the caller is `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")`. This message is inaccurate: the SQL expression feature is implemented (see `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` and `pkg/expr/sql/`), it is deliberately disabled/gated as a security measure (CVE-2024-9264). Telling users it is "not implemented" will cause confusion and incorrect troubleshooting (users may believe the query type is unsupported rather than disabled by configuration). The message should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" or "sqlExpressions feature is disabled" so that operators understand they need to enable the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle (and accept the security implications) to use it.
